factual_problem: Two terminology/role errors. (1) 'unelected analysts and parliamentarians' — in ordinary English a parliamentarian is an elected member of a parliament, so the plural generic reads as false; the referent is the single appointed Senate parliamentarian, as the bullets themselves concede by reverting to 'The parliamentarian'. (2) 'The budget office's economic projections function as gatekeeping determinations that permit or block legislation' misassigns the role: the scorekeeper estimates budgetary effect, while eligibility rulings on what is 'extraneous' are the parliamentarian's — the merge inherited this confusion from originals that claim legislation proceeds 'only for legislation the CBO classifies as budget-related'.
why: Eight near-duplicates collapsing to one note is the right move, but the merge kept the role names and the budget-procedure setting (so it never rises to the transferable principle that whoever certifies technical eligibility for a fast-track acquires substantive veto power), misuses 'parliamentarians', and drops the two mechanisms that gave the originals their force — the vote-free killing of popular provisions and the asymmetric use of scoring assumptions.

All four source claims survive in general form — the help-frame versus know-frame substitution, the caretaker reflex that makes the other person a case study, the role asymmetry that replaced 'the steady nervous system or mirror rather than an equal participant', and the blocked mutual reveal — and the title states a relational principle that reaches mentorship and friendship, not just courtship, with no false or overclaimed assertion left in it.

factual_problem: 'The framing effect' is a named cognitive bias: logically equivalent descriptions of the same option (gain versus loss wording) shift choice. 'Do you want to see me again?' and 'the next chapter of a story that already began' are not equivalent descriptions of one content — they perform different social acts (soliciting consent versus asserting continuation), so the framing effect is not the operative mechanism. Neither original invoked it; the merge introduced the label, and the bullets themselves explain the result through value and status signalling, not frame-dependent choice. The comparative efficacy claim ('stronger', originally 'increases the likelihood of acceptance') is also asserted without support.
why: The merge bought generalizability by borrowing a technical label it has not earned — the title says "The framing effect makes..." while the bullets argue from value signalling ("An offer communicates value when the asker leads with direction") — so it trades the originals' instance-lock for a false causal attribution, and also loses the one actionable mechanism ('when' rather than 'if'); retitle to the signalling claim and the note is sound.

Unlike the audited jealousy/malicious-envy case, this is not a correction — the original title, 'Photographs serve as memory anchors', used the term correctly and the merge broke it.

factual_problem: The note states as a general principle that "Academic freedom limits that authority by protecting peer-facing publication", i.e. an inherent right good against any "employing institution". That is false as stated. Academic freedom is a professional norm enforced through contracts, tenure rules and institutional policy, not a freestanding legal limit on employers; private employers may and routinely do restrict employee publication by contract, and for government employees Garcetti v. Ceballos (2006) holds that speech made pursuant to official duties is not First Amendment-protected, with the scholarship carve-out expressly left open and split in the lower courts. By stripping the three concrete grounds the original relied on (agency policy, First Amendment argument, separation of powers) the merge converted a hedged, context-bound claim into an unsupported doctrinal assertion.
why: The kernel is salvageable — "An employing institution gains administrative authority over workers but does not thereby own every professional judgment they make" is a real and transferable insight — but the second bullet asserts a general legal protection that does not exist, and the generalization is what broke it, so the owner is currently better served by the narrow true original than by this transferable falsehood.

factual_problem: 'Legalistic propaganda depends on ambiguity' inverts the standard sense of legalism, which is strict adherence to the letter of a text against its spirit; legalistic reading characteristically exploits literal wording (contract loopholes, letter-vs-spirit rulings) rather than requiring ambiguity in it. The original asserted only that legalism 'requires acceptance of an external interpretive scheme' — i.e. mediation — which is not the same as ambiguity in the source language, so the generalization is a substitution, not a correction.
why: The merge swapped the original's mechanism (words resonate because they match lived experience, and need no interpretive mediation) for a different and dubious one — 'Legalistic propaganda depends on ambiguity' — which misstates legalism, a doctrine defined by literalism; the salvageable claim is that plain wording denies reframers the room that interpretive mediation needs.

factual_problem: "Person-environment fit" is a borrowed industrial/organizational-psychology construct for person-to-job or person-to-organization congruence, and the title misuses it twice over: fit is a state of congruence, so advice cannot be the thing that makes "person-environment fit fail," and the bullets are in fact about which partner types a technique filters for, not about fit at all.
